sentences.text: The hoopoe starling featured plumage that was primarily white and grey, with darker brown and grey on its back, wings, and tail. It also possessed a light, mobile crest that curled forwards.
Researchers suggest the bird was sexually dimorphic, with males being larger and having more curved beaks. It was the largest of the three Mascarene starlings.
Two specimens from the aviary of Julien Desjardins were sent to the Paris museum in 1839, though the last definite record of a live bird was taken in 1836.
The only known subfossil specimen is a femur discovered in 1993 in a Réunion grotto.
The hoopoe starling reportedly lived in large flocks and inhabited humid areas and marshes. Its robust pelvis, large feet and claws, and strong jaws indicate it foraged near the ground.
The bird was an omnivore that fed on fruits, seeds, and insects.
Researchers suggest a sea-level increase during the last interglacial period may have reduced the hoopoe starling's habitat and caused a population decrease.

In 1831, French naturalist René-Primevère Lesson placed the hoopoe starling in its own monotypic genus, Fregilipus. German ornithologist Hermann Schlegel proposed in 1857 that the bird belonged to the starling family and reclassified it as Sturnus capensis.

Swedish zoologist Carl Jakob Sundevall proposed the genus name Lophopsarus in 1872, but Fregilupus varius remains the valid binomial name as it is the oldest. British zoologist James Murie agreed in 1874 that the hoopoe starling was a starling after analyzing its skeleton.

The hoopoe starling's lineage diverged from other starlings 4 million years ago, suggesting it may have first evolved on now-submerged landmasses. The divergence of the lineage converged with the emergence of Réunion between 2.1 and 3.0 million years ago, without evidence of stepping-stone dispersal.
The species is considered extinct by 1850, making the hoopoe starling the last of the Mascarene starling species to go extinct.

American ornithologist Andrew John Berger cast doubt on the hoopoe starling's relationship with starlings in 1957 due to subtle anatomical differences. Some authors proposed a relationship between the bird and vangas, but this was rejected by Japanese ornithologist Hiroyuki Morioka in 1996. It is debated whether the type illustration of the hoopoe starling was a life drawing or a derivative of an earlier drawing by Jossigny. It is suggested that the introduction of the common myna led to competition with the hoopoe starling.
